                                   LIMITED PROTEST OF
                          EAST KENTUCKY POWER COOPERATIVE, INC.

           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure1 and the

Commission’s August 13, 2026 “Combined Notice of Filings #2,” East Kentucky Power

Cooperative, Inc. (“EKPC”)2 hereby submits this limited protest of the August 13, 2026 filing3 of

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposing revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to

establish an Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”). Under its IRAS Proposal, PJM would

be authorized to direct Electric Distributors to implement load curtailments as a new emergency

procedure step subject to North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) compliance

and provide compensation to the load that is curtailed. To support IRAS, PJM is also proposing in

the IRAS Proposal new definitions for Large Load, New Large Load, and Eligible New Large

Load; the creation of a Large Load Registry; and the exclusion of New Large Loads from the

Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) curve starting in the 2029/2030 Delivery Year.

           EKPC shares the concern that PJM is attempting to address through the establishment of

an IRAS-type service, and supports the curtailing of data center load that connects without it or its

reasonable and could result in the curtailment of load that is supported by capacity resources and

therefore not contributing to the resource adequacy concerns that the IRAS Proposal is intended

to address. Moreover, PJM requiring other loads in the zone not contributing to the need for IRAS

to pay for the IRAS curtailments is not just and reasonable. Finally, PJM’s proposal discriminates

between similarly situated load based solely on whether its LSE satisfies its capacity obligation

through Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) auctions or the Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”)

alternative; the IRAS Proposal compounds the problem by adopting an additional requirement for

FRR Capacity Plans that creates ambiguity and may disadvantage entities that elect FRR in the

future.

           For these reasons, and as discussed herein, the Commission should reject several elements

of PJM’s proposed Tariff and RAA revisions and require appropriate clarifications and revisions

to the IRAS Proposal in order to avoid unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory results.

      I.       Background

           A. IRAS Overview

           As proposed by PJM, IRAS is a supplemental reliability mechanism that addresses the

undisciplined connection of New Large Loads without sufficient capacity being available in the

PJM Region. As explained by PJM, IRAS permits New Large Loads to connect to the PJM system

while managing the capacity shortfall that confronts the PJM Region through targeted, emergency

load reductions and incentives for self-supply of new capacity.4 Fundamentally, as explained by

PJM, “IRAS will enable PJM to prioritize load reduction in zones/areas where New Large Loads

Reliability Backstop Procurement (‘RBP’),” and New Large Loads can avoid IRAS “by bringing

secure sufficient capacity, under the proposed IRAS framework, [give] the ability to manage real-

time operational issues resulting from such shortages through Interim Resource Adequacy Service

Action.”6 The PJM IRAS Proposal is being driven by an acute and worsening resource adequacy

pronged, ongoing effort by PJM to respond to the challenges stemming from the influx of Large

Loads into the PJM Region.”7

           PJM explains that, as part of its IRAS Proposal, it is proposing “three foundational

revisions” in the IRAS Filing. First, PJM is proposing a load reduction mechanism, which

“clarif[ies] a Load Serving Entity’s (‘LSE’) obligation to bring new capacity in an amount that

equals or exceeds its New Large Loads’ peak load or be subject to load reduction requests during

Emergencies prior to Pre-Emergency Load Management Response.”8 As PJM notes, this “lays the

foundation for the IRAS paradigm in PJM.”9 Second, PJM is proposing to establish a Large Load

Registry, which will be “a database of information pertaining to Large Loads that will be

established and maintained by PJM.”10 Third, PJM has proposed that certain New Large Loads

                    1. IRAS Load Reduction Mechanism

           IRAS is a load reduction service, which PJM claims is the “foundation” for IRAS, and will

be available starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year.13 PJM may invoke an IRAS Action when

it determines that available economic real-time supply may be insufficient to maintain reserves,

meet applicable Reserve Requirements and Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits

(“IROLs”), or prevent cascading outages.14 Load reductions under IRAS would be called before

Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions.15 PJM would direct only aggregate MW quantities

of load reduction to the relevant Electric Distributor zone or area; PJM would not identify specific

end-use customers for curtailment.16 Electric Distributors, in coordination with state authorities

and Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities (“RERRAs”), would determine which retail

loads are ultimately reduced, consistent with state-approved curtailment programs.17 As explained

by PJM, this framework reflects a cooperative-federalism model designed to respect the

                   2. Large Load Registry

           PJM proposes to establish a centralized registry of Large Loads in the PJM Region,

maintained by PJM and updated periodically.19 The registry would collect detailed information

including, among other items, peak load quantities, in-service dates, Bring Your Own New

contracts.20 Information would be available – subject to confidentiality protections under

Commission, with aggregated data posted publicly by zone/area.21 PJM claims that the registry

                    3. New Large Load Definitions

           PJM proposes to define “Large Load” as “end-use customer(s) load that has a cumulative

peak load of 50 megawatts or greater at a single electrical site behind one or more points of

interconnection, where for configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple

points of interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them, all affiliated load facilities

within a one-mile radius will be considered a single electrical site as further described in the PJM

Manuals.”24 “New Large Load” is defined separately as “an end-use customer load that is either

(a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after

June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior

to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.” 25 Last, “Eligible

New Large Load” is defined as “a New Large Load eligible to provide Interim Resource Adequacy

Service in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V.”26

                     4. Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”)

           New Large Loads may avoid or reduce their IRAS exposure by contracting with qualifying

new capacity. BYONC is defined as new megawatts of Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”) that meet

specified “gating criteria” to ensure that the capacity is genuinely new – including new-build

generation, qualifying uprates, repowered deactivated resources, qualifying fuel conversions, and

certain new demand-side resources.27 To ensure that the capacity benefits are durable, BYONC

must participate as a price taker ($0/MW offer) in RPM Auctions for ten consecutive Delivery

Years, subject to all capacity market rules.28 A New Large Load’s potential IRAS obligation is

inversely proportional to the amount of BYONC and Allocated RBP UCAP MW it has secured.29

                    5. VRR Curve Exclusion

           Beginning with the 2029/2030 Delivery Year, PJM proposes to exclude incremental New

Large Loads from the VRR Curve to the extent that they do not have sufficient BYONC or

Allocated RBP UCAP MW arrangements.30 Once a New Large Load’s associated BYONC is

offered into the applicable RPM Auction, the corresponding load would be reflected in the demand

curve.31 This measure is intended to protect residential customers from capacity price increases

attributable to large-load additions that have not secured their own capacity.32 It also has the effect

of limiting BYONC to only those resources that clear simultaneously with the New Large Load.

            B. The Stakeholder Process and Joint EDC Proposal

           PJM’s IRAS Proposal emerged from several overlapping stakeholder and PJM Board-

driven processes. On January 16, 2026, the PJM Board issued a letter outlining a multi-pronged

approach to addressing large-load resource adequacy challenges, including a backstop

procurement and cost-allocation mechanisms.33 On March 25, 2026, the Board directed formation

of the Connect and Manage Senior Task Force to develop a framework for connecting large loads

subject to operational controls.34 The PJM Board initiated a Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”)

stakeholder process on April 8, 2026, initially focused on the RBP, the scope of which was later

expanded to include the IRAS framework, concluding that the “substantive link” between RBP

and IRAS warranted a single process.35 The expanded CIFP concluded on June 30, 2026.36

Stakeholders submitted advisory votes on eleven proposals addressing the concepts embodied in

IRAS; none achieved the requisite two-thirds support.37

           Despite this outcome, the PJM Board concluded that the deteriorating resource adequacy

outlook required timely action.38 On July 27, 2026, the Board issued a decisional letter directing

PJM to file the IRAS Proposal as presented.39 The IRAS Proposal is therefore a PJM Board-

directed filing, not a stakeholder-endorsed compromise.40

            EKPC was a co-sponsor of a Connect & Manage proposal (the “Joint EDC Proposal”) that

received 50% stakeholder support.41 The Joint EDC Proposal recognized that “[i]f LSEs take on a

retail obligation to supply Large Loads, as defined by the PJM Tariff, without sufficient capacity

resources to serve them, they impose risk onto the PJM region. It is appropriate to place rules upon

such entities to mitigate that unreasonable risk to others.”42 The Joint EDC Proposal featured some

of the same concepts as PJM’s IRAS Proposal, including a large load registry, a definition of “New

Large Load,” and BYONC resources and determinations.43 But, how the Joint EDC Proposal

proposed to implement these concepts differed in significant ways from PJM’s IRAS Proposal.

II.        Limited Protest

           A. Introduction

           PJM claims that IRAS is necessary “to mitigate the potential reliability risks associated

with resource adequacy” and is a “mechanism to support reliability while allowing New Large

Loads to connect even when new capacity supply lags behind load growth.”44 EKPC shares PJM’s

concern about resource adequacy and the reliability challenges facing the PJM Region, supports

measures that maintain resource adequacy, and recognizes the urgency of PJM’s reliability

concerns. EKPC even supports the idea of an IRAS-type service as evidenced by its sponsorship

of the Joint EDC Proposal. However, as filed, the PJM IRAS Proposal imposes unreasonable

curtailment risk on loads not contributing to the resource adequacy concepts underpinning the

certain elements of the IRAS Proposal are not consistent with requirements of the FPA.

           Key elements of the IRAS Proposal are unjust and unreasonable. First, the IRAS

Proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it fails to recognize an LSE’s existing supply portfolio

in determining whether load will be subject to IRAS. If an RPM Self-Supply LSE has sufficient

resources – either owned or secured through bilateral contracts, whether “new” or existing – to

meet the demand of its load, that load should not risk being subject to the IRAS requirements,

including in particular curtailment. Snapping a line between what is “new” versus “existing” and

ignoring certain resources voids the value that loads relying upon those resources otherwise should

be able to derive. It unreasonably subjects loads that were not contributing to the need for IRAS

to curtailment obligations.

           Second, similarly, PJM has proposed that a BYONC resource must be committed in an

RPM Auction at the same time the New Large Load is included in the RPM Auction in order to

offset IRAS exposure. This requirement creates the potential for disconnects between the

commercial operation date of a BYONC resource, the timeline for the conducting of an RPM

Auction, and full Delivery Year commitment required by RPM Auctions. These potential

disconnects mean that an LSE may have brought real capacity to the system yet the associated load

remains exposed to IRAS. As explained in the Affidavit of Marc Montalvo, as a result of PJM’s

proposal, resources with similar reliability characteristics may receive different treatment under

IRAS.45 This fundamentally undermines the resource adequacy incentives that PJM intends to

create with IRAS and penalizes loads that did not contribute to the need for IRAS.

            Third, it is unreasonable to require specific capacity resources to be devoted to the service

of specific end-consumer large loads. Yet that is what PJM’s IRAS Proposal does since curtailment

exposure may depend on whether UCAP MW from BYONC receives recognition for satisfying

the peak load contribution of a specific Large Load and is tagged to that load through the in-service

lifespan of that specific Large Load.46 As a result, PJM’s IRAS Proposal ignores prudent portfolio

planning and the standard practice of Self-Supply LSEs specifically to develop and manage

resources on a system-wide basis (i.e., for the entirety of their load obligation, not matching

specific resources to specific loads). Mr. Montalvo explains that the “resource-to-load attribution”

required by IRAS is contrary to “longstanding utility planning and operating practice.”47

           Fourth, as proposed, the strict BYONC recognition rules create an unreasonable restriction

on an LSE’s ability to adjust its portfolio. Under PJM’s proposal, BYONC is non-transferable,48

and a BYONC arrangement with New Large Load is permanent “unless and until the New Large

Load is permanently out-of-service.”49 This restriction does not seem to account for the fact that

an LSE may serve multiple loads, and an LSE should have the flexibility it needs to adjust its

portfolio to cover its load obligation, including transferring BYONC.50

           Fifth, PJM has not provided sufficient justification for its broad proposed definition of New

Large Load. For example, PJM’s proposed definition of New Large Load “encompass[es] all end-

use customer(s) load that meet the [certain] requirements.”51 It thus includes commercial and

           Additionally, EKPC seeks clarification as to how PJM intends to measure the MW quantity

it will direct an Electric Distributor to curtail in an IRAS Action. This clarification is necessary to

eliminate a potential unjust and unreasonable result. Specifically, EKPC seeks to avoid PJM

of New Large Loads that exceeds the amount of actual New Large Load demand in real time. Such

a directive from PJM would result in the Electric Distributor having to drop existing customer load

that is not New Large Load. PJM proposes to determine the zonal allocation of IRAS based on the

“total Final RBP Target MW across all zone/areas.”53 Not only does determining the zonal

allocation of IRAS pursuant to this proposal fail to account for whether the Large Load included

in the forecast used in the RPM Auctions, which formed the basis for PJM’s shortfall calculation

setting the RBP Target, actually came to fruition, it also fails to take into consideration whether

that load is actually on line in real-time when PJM is making the decision to issues an IRAS

curtailment directive. Thus, the directive could be expecting an Electric Distributor to curtail an

amount of load that is not only larger than the actual Large Load in the zone but also larger than

the amount of Large Load actually taking service at that moment. Such a directive would create a

conundrum for an Electric Distributor in which it must abide by the Operating Instruction or face

potential NERC compliance consequences. This introduces uncertainty as to whether an Electric

Distributor will need to shed other load beyond the Large Load that IRAS was intended to address.

            PJM has failed to show that compensating IRAS is just and reasonable. PJM has also

not sufficiently demonstrated that compensating IRAS curtailment is warranted. PJM has not

shown why the IRAS curtailment consequence should be converted into a compensable wholesale

service funded by other load.

           Certain elements of the IRAS Proposal are unduly discriminatory. Certain aspects of

the IRAS Proposal are unduly discriminatory because they create an unjustified distinction among

entities that have taken similar resource adequacy actions. As proposed, New Large Loads within

an FRR Service Area cannot be Eligible New Large Loads. In contrast, an RPM Capacity Market

LSE that has likewise prudently planned to serve its load does not receive comparable treatment

under the proposed IRAS framework. As explained in Mr. Montalvo’s Affidavit, this raises

comparability concerns54 and results in undue discrimination between similarly situated

participants in the PJM market.

           Last, the proposal also creates ambiguity for, and potentially disadvantages, entities that

may elect FRR in the future because it introduces new restrictions on the use of existing generation

in an FRR Capacity Plan. PJM’s proposal fails to account for the fact that IRAS may not be in

place in the future, but this restriction on an FRR Capacity Plan would remain.

           In conclusion, PJM’s IRAS Proposal attempts to address a legitimate resource adequacy

need. Key revisions and clarifications, however, are required in order to ensure PJM addresses the

resource adequacy need in a just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory fashion. Therefore,

for the reasons discussed herein, the Commission should reject certain provisions of the IRAS

Proposal and require appropriate revisions and clarifications to address the proposal elements that

would create unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory results.

             B. Elements of PJM’s IRAS Proposal Are Not Just and Reasonable.

          Under Section 205 of the FPA, 16 U.S.C. § 824d, all rates and charges made by a public

utility for the transmission or wholesale sale of electric energy subject to the Commission’s

jurisdiction, and all rules and regulations affecting such rates or charges, “shall be just and

reasonable.”55 A rate or charge that is not just and reasonable “is hereby declared to be unlawful.”56

Section 205(b) further prohibits any public utility from making or granting “any undue preference

or advantage to any person or subject any person to any undue prejudice or disadvantage.” 57 The

burden of proof is on the filing utility to make an affirmative evidentiary showing that the proposed

rates, terms, and conditions satisfy the statutory standard.58 General assertions and policy

aspirations are insufficient, and PJM has failed to meet this burden with respect to certain aspects

of the IRAS Proposal.

                    1. Subjecting LSEs with Sufficient Existing Resources to Cover New Large
                       Load to IRAS is Unjust and Unreasonable.

            PJM’s IRAS Proposal requires all loads satisfying the broad definition of “New Large

Loads” to be subject to IRAS if new capacity resources are not secured for the load-serving

obligation associated with the New Large Load.59 As proposed, LSEs serving New Large Loads

that have prudently planned their (existing) resource portfolios cannot avoid being subject to IRAS

   Resource adequacy is a forward-looking investment and planning function

20. Resource adequacy planning ensures that sufficient resources will be available to serve

   forecast load and maintain reliability standards. Because generation resources often require

   years to permit, finance, construct and interconnect, utilities and other load-serving entities

   make resource development and procurement decisions well before a resource enters service.

   Reliability outcomes depend on investment decisions, contractual commitments, and

   development activities that occur years before commercial operation.

21. Utilities routinely commit capital and organizational resources to projects long before those

   projects satisfy market qualification requirements. Site acquisition, permitting, equipment

IV.      EKPC’s Data Center Tariff and Obligation To Adjust Power Supply Plan

17. In October, 2025, the KY PSC approved EKPC’s Data Center Tariff which applies data centers
    that satisfy two criteria: load size (15 megawatts ("MWs") or greater) and load factor (60% or
    greater). The over-arching goal of the Rate DCP Tariff is to minimize - and if possible
    eliminate - cross-subsidization of data center load and non-data center load. The proposed
    Rate DCP Tariff acknowledges that large data center loads could exceed EKPC's existing
    portfolio of generation resources. Accordingly, the Rate DCP Tariff includes a requirement that
    EKPC will work with a data center to develop and implement a power supply plan to support

     bilateral power and capacity purchases; or a combination of these resources. For those data
     center loads exceeding 250 MWs, one or more Dedicated Resources will be required as part of
     the power supply plan. The Dedicated Resource in EKPC’s data center tariff is an important
     system resource planning requirement, but the Dedicated Resource is not “tied” to a particular
     load as IRAS contemplates. At this time, EKPC has not executed a contract to serve a new data
     center; however, there are several actively negotiating terms and conditions of service utilizing
     our Data Center Tariff framework. The IRAS proposal filed by PJM has created a significant
     headwind to data center investments because it fails to give credit to loads for existing
     resources that are under contract.
18. EKPC’s focus on data centers differs from PJM’s more expansive definition of Large Load that
    includes industrial and manufacturing loads. As noted above, EKPC plans for the growth of
    industrial and manufacturing loads as part of its ongoing forecasting and planning efforts. To
    the extent a data center is under 250 MW, EKPC would ensure its load requirements would be
    satisfied as part of EKPC’s forecasting and portfolio planning efforts. However, data center
    loads greater than 250 MW would require “Dedicated Resources.” This not does mean that
    EKPC deviates from a portfolio approach, but rather that EKPC ensures there are sufficient
    resources to satisfy the data center load and places additional financial obligations directly on
    the data centers to ensure that other loads are protected from costs associated with supplying
    their needs.
